newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia conservatives alarmed by top brass sackings.
newsitem.headline: Russia conservatives alarmed by top brass sackings.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's conservative foes were caught off guard on Thursday by his sacking of Defence Minister Igor Rodionov in a blitz attack which he said opened the way to military reforms.

A senior communist member of the State Duma lower house of parliament said the dismissals of Rodionov and Chief of Staff Viktor Samsonov at a meeting of the advisory Defence Council were unmerited and politically-motivated.

"Rodionov and Samsonov lost their jobs mainly because of their honesty and decency," Viktor Ilyukhin, head of the Duma security committee, told reporters. "Their only fault was that they spoke honestly about the problems of the armed forces."
Yeltsin sacked Rodionov and Samsonov after accusing them of mishandling long-delayed military reforms.

Rodionov has said Russia's armed forces, where some officers have not been paid for months and some ordinary soldiers are poorly fed in remote garrisions, needs much more money if full-scale military reforms are to be carried out.
His main opponent Yuri Baturin, the secretary of the Defence Council, says military reform must be fast and dramatic to save the armed forces from collapse.
Baturin said funds for reform could be raised by optimising the swollen structures of the armed forces and cutting costs.
By sacking Rodionov and his ally, Samsonov, Yeltsin appeared to take the side of Baturin and his new team of young reformist ministers in the protracted argument.
"They (Rodionov and Samsonov) did not fit in with the team of so-called 'young politicians' who are in fact a team of young destroyers," Ilyukhin said.
The nationalist deputy chairman of the Duma, Sergei Baburin, suggested many more sackings would follow.
"We see the start of a disgusting process of a purge in the armed forces," Interfax news agency quoted Baburin as saying.
Ilyukhin suggested the military were not the only ones who could suffer.
"Next to follow are (Interior Minister Anatoly) Kulikov and (Justice Minister Valentin) Kovalyov," Ilyukhin said of two relatively conservative officials strongly backed by parliament.
The reaction of representatives of the top brass who have changed their uniform for parliamentary seats was more reserved, but they also said the victims were not the only ones to blame.
"There was no reason to sack Rodionov," Lev Rokhlin, a retired general who won prominence during the military campaign to crush separatists in rebel Chechnya, told reporters.
"Yeltsin should have approved the plans for reforming the armed forces first and only then demanded their implementation."
Yeltsin, worried by a decline in the badly financed and unduly large armed forces, had ordered Rodionov to carry out reform to turn the Russian army into a tight professional force by the year 2000.
But the Kremlin leader has avoided openly taking sides in the tug-of-war between Rodionov and Baturin.
Yeltsin's foes and allies alike were left asking whether the latest changes would have any benefit.

"The sackings are a clever way to distract public attention from the complete failure of military reform," Interfax quoted retired general Alexander Lebed, a potential presidential candidate in the year 2000, as saying.
